entry.title: Pick and Check an Image-Processing Step
entry.summary: A cheat sheet for parts 3, 4, 7, 8 and 9 - which transform or filter to pick, the number to check by hand, and five labs to try.

entry.title: Pictures and the Middle: Histogram, Polygon, Ogive, and What 'Typical' Means
entry.summary: Draw the table before you summarise it: histogram for amount, polygon for comparison, ogive for up to here. Then "typical" is three questions, mean, median and mode, and none answers two clumps.

entry.title: Samples, Data Types and Tables: Who You Asked, What Kind of Column, How to Count It
entry.summary: A sample speaks for a crowd only if you chose it fairly. The kind of column decides which arithmetic is allowed, and a frequency table counts it without losing the shape, if the drawers touch.

entry.title: Spread and Position: Variance, n − 1, Percentiles, Z-Scores and the Box Plot
entry.summary: Mean, median and mode are three attitudes to how a long walk hurts; spread is the walking left over. A value then has a position only in its crowd: rank (percentile) or distance (z-score).

entry.title: Averages and Intervals: Why Averages Behave and How Sure You Can Be
entry.summary: An average is itself random: its spread shrinks as sigma over root n and its shape tends to a bell. A confidence interval turns that wobble into a give-or-take, and bias is invisible to it.

entry.title: Counting and Conditioning: Why a 99% Accurate Test Is Usually Wrong
entry.summary: Probability is a share of the equally likely ways, so "or" adds, "and" multiplies and "at least one" is 1 minus none. Conditioning shrinks the crowd, and Bayes' rule reads that count backwards.

entry.title: Expectation and the Two Count Recipes: Binomial and Poisson
entry.summary: Expected value is the data's seesaw with probability as the weight, not the likeliest outcome. Binomial and Poisson are recipes for a count; each is right only as far as its assumptions hold.

entry.title: Summarise a Data Set: Which Number, Which Picture
entry.summary: A cheat sheet for parts 1 to 6 - choose a sampling method, classify the data, pick the picture, pick the middle and the spread, and place one value in its crowd.

entry.title: Describing Data, Technically: Definitions, Identities and Method Choices
entry.summary: The formal layer under parts 1 to 6: scales of measurement, grouped-data formulas, what the mean and median minimise, n versus n-1, quartile methods, fences and sampling designs.

entry.title: From a Sample to a Statement: Intervals, Tests and Lines

entry.title: Inference, Technically: Sampling Distributions, Intervals, Tests and Regression
entry.summary: The formal layer under parts 12 to 15: the sampling distribution of the mean, intervals and the t distribution, p-values and permutation tests, multiple testing, and least-squares regression.

entry.title: Pick and Compute the Right Probability Model
entry.summary: A cheat sheet for parts 7 to 11 - the method, the code and the expected output for counting outcomes, flipping a test result, expected value, binomial or Poisson, and the normal curve.
